topic.subject: science
topic.title: Is matter around us pure
topic.scope: mixtures vs compounds, solutions, suspensions, colloids, concentration, separation techniques, elements

misconceptions.statement: A substance is pure if it is natural and contains no harmful additives.
misconceptions.why: Students use the everyday marketing definition of 'pure' (like pure ghee or milk) instead of the chemical one.
misconceptions.fix: In chemistry, a pure substance consists of only one type of particle (atoms or molecules) with the same chemical nature.

probe.question: Is full-cream milk a pure substance in chemistry?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it comes directly from the cow without adding water.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

misconceptions.statement: If a mixture looks uniform and clear to the naked eye, it must be a pure substance.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on macroscopic visual evidence to determine microscopic composition.
misconceptions.fix: Homogeneous mixtures like salt solutions look uniform but contain different types of particles that can be separated physically.

probe.question: You are given a clear, colorless liquid. Can you conclude it is a pure substance?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because I cannot see any different parts in it.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: A solute must always be a solid and a solvent must always be a liquid.
misconceptions.why: The most common examples taught (salt in water) become the prototype for all solutions.
misconceptions.fix: Solutions can exist in any state; for example, air is a gas-in-gas solution and brass is a solid-in-solid solution.

probe.question: In the alloy brass (zinc and copper), which one is the solvent?
probe.wrong_answer: Neither, because they are both solids and solutions must be liquid.

misconceptions.root_belief: a prototype represents the entire category

misconceptions.statement: Colloids are homogeneous mixtures because they do not settle over time.
misconceptions.why: Students equate stability and lack of visible settling with homogeneity.
misconceptions.fix: Colloids are heterogeneous because the particle size is large enough to scatter light, even if they don't settle.

probe.question: Why is milk classified as a heterogeneous mixture even though it looks uniform?
probe.wrong_answer: It is actually homogeneous because the fat doesn't settle at the bottom.

misconceptions.statement: Concentration is calculated by dividing the mass of solute by the mass of the solvent.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the 'solvent' with the 'total solution' in the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: Mass percentage is (Mass of Solute / Mass of Solution) × 100, where solution mass is solute + solvent.

probe.question: If 10g of salt is added to 100g of water, what is the mass of the solution used in the denominator?

misconceptions.root_belief: the whole is the same as the largest part

misconceptions.statement: A saturated solution is 'full' and cannot dissolve any other substance.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'saturated' means the solvent has no space left for any particles at all.
misconceptions.fix: A solution saturated with one solute can still dissolve a different solute.

probe.question: If a solution is saturated with salt, can it dissolve any sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the solution is already saturated and full.

misconceptions.root_belief: a limit for one thing is a limit for all

misconceptions.statement: When a solution evaporates, the solute also disappears or turns into gas.
misconceptions.why: Students often believe that when the liquid 'goes away', the whole mixture is gone.
misconceptions.fix: Evaporation only removes the volatile solvent; the non-volatile solute is left behind as a solid.

probe.question: What happens to the salt when a salt-water solution is heated to dryness?
probe.wrong_answer: The salt evaporates along with the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: matter disappears when it changes state
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: A compound has the same properties as the elements it is made from.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the nature of mixtures (which retain properties) with compounds.
misconceptions.fix: A compound has entirely different properties from its constituent elements.

probe.question: Since Hydrogen and Oxygen are gases, why is water (H2O) a liquid at room temperature?
probe.wrong_answer: Water must actually be a gas that we see as liquid, or it must act like a gas.

misconceptions.root_belief: the whole is just the sum of its parts

misconceptions.statement: Distillation and boiling are the same process.
misconceptions.why: Both involve heating a liquid to its boiling point, so students miss the condensation step.
misconceptions.fix: Boiling is just a phase change; distillation is a separation technique involving both evaporation and condensation.

probe.question: Can you perform distillation using only a heater and an open beaker?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because distillation is just boiling the liquid.

misconceptions.root_belief: one part of a process defines the whole

misconceptions.statement: Compounds can be separated into their elements by physical methods like filtration or distillation.
misconceptions.why: Students do not distinguish between the physical bonds in a mixture and chemical bonds in a compound.
misconceptions.fix: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical or electrochemical reactions.

probe.question: How can we separate Hydrogen gas from water?
probe.wrong_answer: By filtering the water through a very fine filter paper.

misconceptions.root_belief: all mixtures and compounds are separated the same way

misconceptions.statement: The Tyndall effect is caused by the liquid itself reflecting light.
misconceptions.why: Students don't realize it is the suspended particles, not the medium, that scatter light.
misconceptions.fix: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by medium-sized colloidal particles.

probe.question: Why do we see the path of light in a forest on a misty morning?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the air itself is glowing.

misconceptions.root_belief: the medium and the object are the same

misconceptions.statement: Mixtures have a fixed melting and boiling point just like pure substances.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the property of 'matter' having fixed points to all forms of matter.
misconceptions.fix: Mixtures do not have fixed melting/boiling points; they melt or boil over a range of temperatures depending on composition.

probe.question: Does salt water always boil at exactly 100 degrees Celsius?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because water is the main part and its boiling point is fixed.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule for a part applies to the whole

misconceptions.statement: Centrifugation works by making the heavier particles lighter so they can float.
misconceptions.why: Students observe separation but misinterpret the physics of density and force.
misconceptions.fix: Centrifugation uses rapid rotation to force denser particles to the bottom and lighter particles to the top.

probe.question: In a cream separator, why does the cream collect at the top?
probe.wrong_answer: The machine spins so fast that the cream becomes weightless and floats.

misconceptions.root_belief: motion changes the intrinsic properties of matter

misconceptions.statement: Chromatography only works for separating colors.
misconceptions.why: The name 'chroma' (color) and the common ink experiment lead to this narrow view.
misconceptions.fix: Chromatography separates any solutes that dissolve in the same solvent but move at different speeds, even colorless ones.

probe.question: Can chromatography be used to separate different colorless drugs in a blood sample?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because chromatography only works if the substances have different colors.

misconceptions.root_belief: the name of a process limits its function

misconceptions.statement: Alloys are compounds because they cannot be separated by simple filtration.
misconceptions.why: Students think if you can't filter it, it must be chemically bonded.
misconceptions.fix: Alloys are mixtures because they show the properties of their constituents and have variable composition, even if they require melting to separate.

probe.question: Why is brass considered a mixture and not a compound?
probe.wrong_answer: It is actually a compound because you cannot see the zinc and copper separately.

misconceptions.root_belief: difficulty of separation defines the type of matter
